Vignette:
# Rajesh's Reckoning

Rajesh Mehta was thirty-two when the bomb went off at the downtown transit station. He had been waiting on the platform for the northbound train, reviewing notes for a therapy session scheduled that afternoon—a routine Tuesday in October that would hollow out the next five years of his life. The blast threw him backward into a concrete pillar. He remembered the sound before the pain: a crack that seemed to split the world open, followed by screaming that didn't feel human. When he regained consciousness in the hospital, his left arm was bandaged and his hearing in his right ear was diminished, but he was alive. Seventeen others were not.

In the months after, Rajesh had returned to his practice at the community mental health clinic with what he believed was resilience. His wife, Priya, was relieved to have him back at work. His colleagues remarked on his composure. But something fundamental had shifted in how he moved through the world. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt absolute, that he could not prevent terrible things from happening—not to himself, not to anyone. The bomb had taught him that control was an illusion, that safety was a story people told themselves. The man he had been before October—the one who believed in the efficacy of talk therapy, in the possibility of change through insight and effort—felt like someone else entirely, someone naïve and foolish.

The nighttime became unbearable first. Rajesh would lie awake beside Priya, unable to sleep, his mind cycling through scenarios of catastrophe. When exhaustion finally pulled him under, he would jolt awake in the dark, his body flooded with adrenaline, certain that something was coming. He began leaving lights on throughout the house. When Priya asked him to turn them off, he couldn't explain the panic that rose in his throat at the prospect of darkness. He had started drinking bourbon most nights—just enough to blunt the edge, to make sleep possible. It had become a ritual, something he depended on. Loud noises sent him reeling. A car backfiring on the street outside his office caused him to drop a pen and grip the armrest of his chair so hard his knuckles whitened. His patients noticed. One had asked if he was all right. The question had mortified him. He was supposed to be the stable presence in the room, the one who held space for others' suffering. Instead, he was barely holding himself together. His startle response had become so pronounced that even the notification sound on his phone could send his heart racing, his palms slick with sweat.

By thirty-seven, Rajesh had begun avoiding anything that felt remotely unpredictable or stressful. He turned down invitations to social events, canceled standing plans with friends, stopped attending the community temple where he and Priya had been married. He told himself these things were unnecessary, that they were just sources of potential threat. His world had contracted to a narrow corridor: home, the clinic, the drive between them. Even at work, he had begun to limit his caseload, referring away patients with trauma histories because their stories triggered a vertigo he couldn't manage. He sat through sessions feeling distant from his own profession, as if watching himself perform the role of psychologist from behind glass. The consequences had become undeniable. His supervisor had gently suggested he consider a leave of absence; the clinic director had expressed concern about his declining patient load and the impact on the department's capacity. Priya had stopped inviting her sister over for dinner, had stopped mentioning gatherings with her family, had learned to move through their home as though navigating around his invisible boundaries.

The alcohol had escalated. A glass of bourbon became two, then a third. Priya had found him asleep on the couch at nine in the evening more than once, an empty bottle on the side table. She had asked him, gently at first and then with visible frustration, what was happening to him. He couldn't answer. How could he tell her that the person she had married—the thoughtful, engaged man who had wanted to help people heal—had been replaced by someone hollow and afraid, someone who spent half his day in a dissociative fog, drifting into fantasy scenarios where he had somehow changed that October morning, where he had taken a different train, where the bomb had never been built? It was Priya who finally insisted he seek help. She had found him researching substances on his laptop at three in the morning, his speech slurred, his pupils dilated. She had wept, not from anger but from grief—grief for the man he had been, for the marriage that was slowly becoming a careful choreography around his avoidance. Rajesh had resisted at first. How could he, a psychologist, admit to needing therapy? But the weight of his own unrecognizability had become too much. He was no longer certain who he was or what he was capable of. He was terrified of the darkness, of loud noises, of sudden sounds, of the possibility that at any moment, without warning, everything could shatter again. And he was more afraid still of the person he was becoming in his attempts to outrun that terror.
